steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting Cole, our hierarchical system for generating multi-layered, editable graphic designs from user intentions. Explain why graphic design generation matters, where current text-to-image models like DALL-E 3 fall short, how our system is structured, and how we evaluate it.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The quality of natural image generation has improved remarkably lately, up to the level of professional photography. This leap is thanks to the development of technologies such as Imagen, SDXL, and DALL \cdot E3. The main factors behind these advances include using a powerful Large Language Model (LLM) as the text encoder, scaling up the training datasets, more model complexity, designing advanced sampling strategies, and better data quality, among others. We think now is the right moment to turn our efforts to more professional image generation, in particular graphic design generation, since it plays a pivotal role in advertising, branding, and marketing.

Graphic design is a professional discipline that uses the power of visual communication to convey targeted messages to specific social groups, with clear objectives. It is an area that needs creativity, innovation, and lateral thinking. Usually graphic design uses manual or digital tools to combine text and graphics and create compelling visual narratives. Its main goal is to structure information, give substance to ideas, and put expression and emotion into artifacts that record human experiences. Graphic design often uses the artistry of typography, text composition, ornamentation, and imagery to convey thoughts, emotions, and attitudes that go beyond what language alone can do. So it needs a high degree of creativity, innovation, and lateral thinking to make top-tier designs.

A very recent study showed empirically that DALL \cdot E3 has impressive capabilities in generating high-quality design images, with visually striking graphics and layouts, as shown in Figure 2. But these images still have flaws. There are several critical challenges, such as mis-rendered visual text, which often ends up with missing or extra characters, something that was also noted in earlier work. Also, editing these generated images needs complex operations like segmentation, erasing, inpainting, and others, because the images are inherently not editable. Another big limitation is that users need to provide detailed text prompts, and in graphic design generation writing effective prompts usually needs a lot of professional expertise. Unlike DALL \cdot E3, our Cole system, shown in Figure 1, can generate multi-layered and editable graphic design images from simple user intentions.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The quality of natural image generation has improved remarkably lately, up to the level of professional photography. This leap is thanks to the development of technologies such as Imagen, SDXL, and DALL \cdot E3. The main factors behind these advances include using a powerful Large Language Model (LLM) as the text encoder, scaling up the training datasets, more model complexity, designing advanced sampling strategies, and better data quality, among others. We think now is the right moment to turn our efforts to more professional image generation, in particular graphic design generation, since it plays a pivotal role in advertising, branding, and marketing.

Graphic design is a professional discipline that uses the power of visual communication to convey targeted messages to specific social groups, with clear objectives. It is an area that needs creativity, innovation, and lateral thinking. Usually graphic design uses manual or digital tools to combine text and graphics and create compelling visual narratives. Its main goal is to structure information, give substance to ideas, and put expression and emotion into artifacts that record human experiences. Graphic design often uses the artistry of typography, text composition, ornamentation, and imagery to convey thoughts, emotions, and attitudes that go beyond what language alone can do. So it needs a high degree of creativity, innovation, and lateral thinking to make top-tier designs.

A very recent study showed empirically that DALL \cdot E3 has impressive capabilities in generating high-quality design images, with visually striking graphics and layouts, as shown in Figure 2. But these images still have flaws. There are several critical challenges, such as mis-rendered visual text, which often ends up with missing or extra characters, something that was also noted in earlier work. Also, editing these generated images needs complex operations like segmentation, erasing, inpainting, and others, because the images are inherently not editable. Another big limitation is that users need to provide detailed text prompts, and in graphic design generation writing effective prompts usually needs a lot of professional expertise. Unlike DALL \cdot E3, our Cole system, shown in Figure 1, can generate multi-layered and editable graphic design images from simple user intentions.

We think these three limitations seriously hurt the quality of the generated graphic design images. A scalable, high-quality graphic design generation system should ideally need minimal effort from users, produce accurate and high-quality typography information for different purposes, and give a flexible editing space. This way users can refine the output further and add human expertise when needed.

Our goal in this work is to build an efficient and dependable autonomous text-to-design system that can generate high-quality graphic design images from user intent prompts. We propose to break down the complex process of graphic design image generation into a hierarchical generation process. This process has multiple specialized generation models, and each one handles a different sub-task. First, we train a Design-LLM to understand vague intentions and do design-oriented planning tasks. We formulate this as a text-to-JSON prediction task, where naive and sparse user intentions have to be transformed into structured, layer-wise captions or attributes that are needed for the task decomposition that follows. Second, for design-oriented visual reasoning and generation, we train three more models. (i) A text-to-background diffusion model to generate the background layer. Here it is crucial that the generated background images leave enough space for adding various elements, which is different from conventional methods like DALL \cdot E3 that often produce objects filling the whole image space. (ii) A text-to-object diffusion model to generate the object layer. The model needs to understand both the content and the style of the background image, and then it should generate an object layer that matches the style and is also put in logical positions. (iii) A Typography-LMM for typography prediction, which has to predict 15 distinct typography attributes for each text box. This part needs a sophisticated level of reasoning about the visual contents of the merged background and object image layers, and then it predicts the typography attributes based on that. We also show that our Typography-LLM generalizes by applying it to processed design images that were originally generated with DALL \cdot E3. See Figure 1 for the visual results. We also introduce a feedback and quality assurance process to improve the quality.

Last, to assess the capability of our system, we construct DesignerIntention, which has \sim 500 professional graphic design intention prompts covering diverse categories and \sim 50 creative ones. We use it to compare our method with the existing state-of-the-art image generation system, run thorough ablation experiments for each generation model on the different sub-tasks, give a detailed analysis of the graphic designs our system creates, and discuss both the limitations and possible future directions of graphic design image generation. Figure 3 shows that for both non-designers and designers our Cole system beats DALL \cdot E3 in text fidelity and message conveyance, with win rates of 69.6% and 70.5%, respectively. For visual appeal, non-designers slightly prefer Cole, while designers prefer DALL \cdot E3. Designers also prefer our results over the ones from the latest commercial product, CanvaGPT. Table 1 gives a detailed comparison of the key differences between our approach, earlier text-to-image generation models, and the latest CanvaGPT. In addition, we report GPT4-V scores from various perspectives, where Cole is better than the others in three critical areas: layout, image, and typography quality.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The recent advancement in the quality of natural image generation has been remarkable, raising it to the level of professional photography. This leap can be attributed to the development of technologies such as Imagen [1], SDXL [2], and DALL \cdot E3 [3]. The key factors behind these advances include the use of a powerful Large Language Model (LLM) as the text encoder, the scaling up of training datasets, increased model complexity, the design of advanced sampling strategies, and improved data quality, among others. We believe that now is the right moment to redirect our efforts towards more professional image generation, particularly graphic design generation, given its pivotal role in advertising, branding, and marketing.

Graphic design [4] is a professional discipline that leverages visual communication to convey targeted messages to specific social groups, with clear objectives. It is a realm that requires creativity, innovation, and lateral thinking. Typically, graphic design uses either manual or digital tools to combine text and graphics, creating compelling visual narratives. Its primary goal is to structure information, give substance to ideas, and infuse expression and emotion into artifacts that chronicle human experiences. Graphic design often relies on the artistry of typography, text composition, ornamentation, and imagery to convey thoughts, emotions, and attitudes that go beyond the capabilities of language alone. In essence, producing top-tier designs demands a high degree of creativity, innovation, and lateral thinking.

The most recent study [5] has empirically shown that DALL \cdot E3 exhibits impressive capabilities in generating high-quality design images, with visually striking graphics and layouts, as illustrated in Figure 2. However, these images are not without flaws. They still face several critical challenges, such as mis-rendered visual text, often with missing or extra characters, a phenomenon also highlighted in [3]. Furthermore, because the generated images are inherently uneditable, editing them demands complex operations such as segmentation, erasing, inpainting, and others. Another substantial limitation is that users must provide detailed text prompts, and developing effective prompts for graphic design generation typically requires a high degree of professional expertise. In contrast to DALL \cdot E3, our Cole system, as shown in Figure 1, can generate multi-layered and editable graphic design images from simple user intentions.

We maintain that these three limitations critically undermine the quality of generated graphic design images. A scalable, high-quality graphic design generation system should ideally require minimal effort from users, produce accurate and high-quality typography information for a variety of purposes, and offer a flexible editing space, allowing users to further refine the output and integrate human expertise when necessary.

Our objective in this work is to establish an efficient and dependable autonomous text-to-design system capable of generating high-quality graphic design images from user intent prompts. We propose breaking down the complex process of graphic design image generation into a hierarchical generation process involving multiple specialized generation models, each handling a different sub-task. First, we train a Design-LLM to comprehend vague intentions and carry out design-oriented planning tasks. We formulate this as a text-to-JSON prediction task, which transforms naive and sparse user intentions into structured, layer-wise captions or attributes essential for the subsequent task decomposition. Second, to perform design-oriented visual reasoning and generation, we train three additional models: (i) a text-to-background diffusion model for background layer generation, which must ensure that the generated background images reserve adequate space for various elements, unlike conventional methods such as DALL \cdot E3 that often produce objects filling the entire image space; (ii) a text-to-object diffusion model for object layer generation, which must understand both the content and style of the background image and then generate an object layer that is stylistically aligned and placed in logical positions; (iii) a Typography-LMM for typography prediction, which predicts 15 distinct typography attributes for each text box. This component requires sophisticated reasoning about the visual contents of the merged background and object image layers before predicting the typography attributes. We also demonstrate the generalization capability of our Typography-LLM by applying it to processed design images originally generated with DALL \cdot E3 (see Figure 1 for the visual results). In addition, we introduce a feedback and quality assurance process to enhance quality.

Last, to assess the capability of our system, we construct DesignerIntention, which consists of \sim 500 professional graphic design intention prompts covering diverse categories and \sim 50 creative ones. We use it to compare our method with the existing state-of-the-art image generation system, conduct thorough ablation experiments for each generation model on the different sub-tasks, offer a detailed analysis of the graphic designs created by our system, and discuss both the limitations and the prospective future directions of graphic design image generation. Figure 3 shows that, among both non-designers and designers, our Cole system outperforms DALL \cdot E3 in text fidelity and message conveyance, achieving win rates of 69.6% and 70.5%, respectively. In terms of visual appeal, non-designers show a slight preference for Cole, while designers favor DALL \cdot E3. Designers also prefer our results over those of the latest commercial product, CanvaGPT. Table 1 provides a detailed comparison of the key differences between our approach, earlier text-to-image generation models, and the latest CanvaGPT. Additionally, we present GPT4-V scores from various perspectives, with Cole outperforming the others in three critical areas: layout, image, and typography quality.

References:
[1] Jia Deng, Wei Dong, Richard Socher, Li-Jia Li, Kai Li, and Li Fei-Fei. Imagenet: A large-scale hierarchical image database. In CVPR , 2009.
[2] Dustin Podell, Zion English, Kyle Lacey, Andreas Blattmann, Tim Dockhorn, Jonas Müller, Joe Penna, and Robin Rombach. Sdxl: Improving latent diffusion models for high-resolution image synthesis. arXiv preprint arXiv:2307.01952 , 2023.
[3] James Betker, Gabriel Goh, Li Jing, Tim Brooks, Jianfeng Wang, Linjie Li, Long Ouyang, Juntang Zhuang, Joyce Lee, Yufei Guo, Wesam Manassra, Prafulla Dhariwal, Casey Chu, Yunxin Jiao, and Aditya Ramesh. Improving image generation with better captions. In OPENAI , 2023.
[4] Wikipedia contributors. Graphic design, 2023a. [Online; accessed 30 October 2023].
[5] Lin Kevin, Yang Zhengyuan, Li Linjie, Wang Jianfeng, and Wang Lijuan. Designbench: Exploring and benchmarking dall-e 3 for imagining visual design. arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.15144 , 2023.
